Artificial intelligence · Machine learning

Supervised learning: classification and regression

How machines learn a mapping from inputs to outputs using labelled examples: the problem, its two-century history, the core algorithms, the theory of generalisation, and how to evaluate a model honestly.

Technical article with worked examples, Python code and exercisesReferences: Vancouver style

Abstract

Supervised learning estimates a function from a finite sample of input–output pairs so that it predicts well on inputs it has not seen. When is a set of categories the task is classification; when it is regression. This article sets out the statistical framing (loss, risk and empirical risk minimisation), traces the history from least squares in 1805 to modern ensembles and deep networks, and develops the main model families: linear and logistic regression, nearest neighbours, decision trees and ensembles, support vector machines, and neural networks. It then treats generalisation (the bias–variance trade-off and regularisation) and evaluation (cross-validation and metrics). Every algorithm comes with runnable Python, and the article closes with ten exercises with full solutions.

1The supervised learning problem

Machine learning is commonly defined as the study of computer programs that improve their performance at some task through experience [1]. In supervised learning the experience takes a specific form: a training set of examples , where each input (a vector of features, also called predictors or covariates) is paired with a known output (the label, target or response). The goal is a function that predicts accurately for new drawn from the same source [2,3]. The word "supervised" refers to the labels: a teacher has supplied the right answer for each training input, in contrast to unsupervised learning, where only the are given [2].

Definition

Classification: the output is a discrete label, . Examples: whether a tumour is malignant or benign, which digit a handwritten image shows, whether an email is spam.
Regression: the output is a real number, . Examples: a house price, a patient's disease progression score after one year, tomorrow's electricity demand.

The two tasks share almost all of their machinery. Many algorithms (trees, nearest neighbours, neural networks, support vector machines) have both a classification and a regression form, and the main difference is the loss function used to score predictions [2,4].

Loss, risk and empirical risk minimisation

Assume the pairs are drawn independently from an unknown joint distribution . A loss function scores the cost of predicting when the truth is . The quantity we would like to minimise is the risk (expected loss, or generalisation error):

Because is unknown, we minimise its sample average, the empirical risk, over a chosen family of functions (the hypothesis class):

This principle, empirical risk minimisation (ERM), was analysed by Vapnik and Chervonenkis, who showed that the gap between and can be bounded uniformly over in terms of its capacity, measured by the VC dimension [5,6]. The optional penalty is regularisation, which trades a little training fit for lower variance (Section 9) [7].

For squared loss the risk-minimising function is the conditional mean, . For 0–1 loss in classification it is the Bayes classifier, which picks the most probable class, ; its error rate, the Bayes rate, is the lowest any classifier can achieve [2,3]. Every method in this article can be read as a different way of approximating one of these two targets from finite data. No single method wins on every problem: averaged over all possible data-generating distributions, all learning algorithms have the same expected off-training-set error, a result known as the "no free lunch" theorem [8].

2A short history

Supervised learning grew out of statistics long before it became a branch of artificial intelligence. Its first algorithm, least squares, was invented to fit the orbits of comets.

  1. 1805Adrien-Marie Legendre publishes the method of least squares in an appendix on comet orbits [9]. Carl Friedrich Gauss publishes it in 1809, claims to have used it since 1795, and links it to normally distributed errors, starting a famous priority dispute [10,11].
  2. 1886Francis Galton studies the heights of parents and children and describes "regression towards mediocrity", giving the method its name [12].
  3. 1936Ronald Fisher introduces the linear discriminant for separating species of iris from four flower measurements; the iris data remain a standard classification example [13].
  4. 1944Joseph Berkson coins the term "logit" and argues for the logistic function in bio-assay [14]. In 1958 David Cox sets out logistic regression for binary outcomes [15].
  5. 1951Evelyn Fix and Joseph Hodges propose the nearest-neighbour rule for nonparametric discrimination [16]. In the same year Robbins and Monro publish the stochastic approximation method that underlies stochastic gradient descent [17].
  6. 1958Frank Rosenblatt describes the perceptron, a trainable linear threshold unit [18]. Widrow and Hoff's ADALINE and its least-mean-squares rule follow in 1960 [19].
  7. 1959Arthur Samuel's checkers program, which improves by experience, helps popularise the phrase "machine learning" [20].
  8. 1967Cover and Hart prove that the asymptotic error of the 1-nearest-neighbour rule is at most twice the Bayes error [21].
  9. 1969Minsky and Papert's Perceptrons shows the limits of single-layer networks, which cannot represent functions such as XOR, and research on neural networks slows [22].
  10. 1970Hoerl and Kennard introduce ridge regression for ill-conditioned least-squares problems [23]. In 1971 Vapnik and Chervonenkis lay the foundations of statistical learning theory [5].
  11. 1974Mervyn Stone formalises cross-validation for choosing and assessing predictors [24].
  12. 1984Breiman, Friedman, Olshen and Stone publish CART (classification and regression trees) [25]. Quinlan's ID3 (1986) and C4.5 (1993) develop trees from the machine learning side [26,27].
  13. 1986Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams popularise back-propagation for training multilayer networks [28]. In 1989 Cybenko and Hornik and colleagues prove that one hidden layer suffices to approximate any continuous function [29,30].
  14. 1992Boser, Guyon and Vapnik combine maximum-margin classifiers with kernels [31]; Cortes and Vapnik's soft-margin "support-vector networks" follow in 1995 [32].
  15. 1996Tibshirani introduces the lasso [33], and Breiman introduces bagging [34]. Freund and Schapire's AdaBoost appears in journal form in 1997 [35].
  16. 2001Breiman publishes random forests [36] and Friedman publishes gradient boosting machines [37].
  17. 2011The scikit-learn library makes these methods available behind one consistent Python interface [38].
  18. 2012A deep convolutional network trained on GPUs wins the ImageNet image-classification challenge with a top-5 error of 15.3%, against 26.2% for the next entry, and sets off the deep learning era [39,40].
  19. 2016XGBoost, a scalable implementation of gradient-boosted trees, becomes a standard tool for tabular data [41]. Trees still often beat deep networks on medium-sized tabular benchmarks [42].

3Loss functions

The loss function encodes what "a good prediction" means, and the choice of loss largely determines the algorithm. Table 1 lists the most common choices. For classification it helps to write the label as and the model's real-valued score as ; the product is the margin, which is positive when the prediction is correct [2].

4Linear regression

Linear regression models the response as a weighted sum of the features plus noise, . Absorbing the intercept into by adding a constant feature of 1, and stacking the inputs as rows of the design matrix , ordinary least squares (OLS) minimises the residual sum of squares:

The middle equations are the normal equations, obtained by setting the gradient to zero. The closed form requires to be invertible; in practice one solves the system with a QR or singular value decomposition rather than forming the inverse [2]. Two classical justifications support OLS. If the noise is Gaussian, least squares is the maximum-likelihood estimate [3,10]. Under the weaker Gauss–Markov conditions (zero-mean, uncorrelated, equal-variance errors), OLS has the smallest variance among all linear unbiased estimators [2].

Gradient descent

When or is large, or when the loss has no closed-form minimiser, parameters are found iteratively. Gradient descent, which goes back to Cauchy in 1847 [44], repeats with a step size (learning rate) . Stochastic gradient descent replaces the full gradient with the gradient on one example or a small mini-batch; this noisy estimate is unbiased, and with suitably decreasing step sizes the iterates converge [17]. Mini-batch SGD and adaptive variants such as Adam are the standard way to train neural networks [45,46].

Both methods recover the same coefficients, close to the true intercept 3 and slope 2. The training mean squared error is near the noise variance , as expected for a correctly specified model. Linear regression is far more flexible than the name suggests: replacing by basis functions such as polynomials , splines or interactions gives non-linear fits that are still linear in the parameters [2,3].

5Logistic regression and linear classifiers

For a binary label , logistic regression models the probability of the positive class by passing a linear score through the logistic sigmoid [3,15]:

The last identity says that the log-odds (the logit) is linear in the features, so each coefficient is the change in log-odds per unit change of its feature [4]. The parameters are fitted by maximum likelihood, which is the same as minimising the average cross-entropy (log loss):

This objective is convex, so gradient methods reach the global minimum, but there is no closed-form solution; classical software uses Newton's method, known in this setting as iteratively reweighted least squares [2]. If the classes are perfectly separable, the unpenalised weights grow without bound, which is one reason to add a penalty [3]. For classes, the softmax function generalises the sigmoid; this is multinomial logistic regression, and it is also the output layer of most neural-network classifiers [45].

The decision boundary of logistic regression is a hyperplane, so it belongs to the family of linear classifiers, along with Fisher's linear discriminant [13], the perceptron [18] and the linear SVM [32]. They differ in how they choose the hyperplane. The perceptron updates whenever it misclassifies an example and is guaranteed to converge only when the data are linearly separable. Logistic regression yields calibrated probabilities. The SVM maximises the margin.

6k-nearest neighbours

The k-nearest-neighbour (k-NN) rule makes no assumption about the form of . To predict at a query point it finds the training points closest to it, usually in Euclidean distance, and returns the majority class (classification) or the mean response (regression) of those neighbours [2,16]. There is no training step beyond storing the data, so k-NN is called a lazy or instance-based learner [1].

The number of neighbours controls flexibility. With the boundary follows every training point and the training error is zero; larger averages over more points and gives smoother boundaries (Figure 5). Cover and Hart showed that, as , the error of the 1-NN rule satisfies , where is the Bayes error and the number of classes. So half of the classification information in an infinite sample is contained in the nearest neighbour [21].

Two practical points matter. First, distances depend on scale, so features should be standardised before applying k-NN. Second, k-NN suffers badly from the curse of dimensionality: in high dimensions almost all points are far from each other, and a neighbourhood that captures a fixed fraction of the data must span most of the range of each feature, so "local" averaging is no longer local [2].

7Decision trees and ensembles

Decision trees

A decision tree splits the feature space into rectangles by asking a sequence of yes/no questions of the form "is ?". Each leaf predicts a constant: the majority class for classification, or the mean response for regression [25]. Trees are grown greedily from the top. At each node the algorithm searches all features and thresholds for the split that most reduces the impurity of the child nodes. For a node whose class proportions are , the two standard impurity measures are [25,26]:

The reduction in entropy produced by a split is the information gain used by ID3 and C4.5 [26,27]; CART uses the Gini index for classification and squared error for regression [25]. A fully grown tree fits the training data almost perfectly and overfits, so trees are limited by a maximum depth or minimum leaf size, or grown fully and then pruned back using cost-complexity pruning [25].

Trees are easy to interpret, handle mixed feature types, need no scaling, and capture interactions. Their weakness is instability: a small change in the data can produce a very different tree, so a single tree has high variance [2,34]. Ensembles turn that weakness into a strength.

Bagging and random forests

Bagging (bootstrap aggregating) trains models on bootstrap resamples of the training set and averages their predictions or takes a majority vote [34]. If each tree has variance and the pairwise correlation between trees is , the variance of their average is [2]. Adding trees removes the second term, but the first remains. Random forests reduce by also choosing a random subset of features as split candidates at each node [36]. About 37% of examples are left out of each bootstrap sample (the fraction tends to ), and predicting each example with only the trees that did not see it gives a nearly free "out-of-bag" error estimate [2,36].

Boosting

Boosting builds an ensemble sequentially, with each new weak learner concentrating on the examples the current ensemble gets wrong. AdaBoost reweights the training examples after each round and combines the learners with weights based on their accuracy [35]. Friedman, Hastie and Tibshirani later showed that AdaBoost performs stagewise additive modelling under the exponential loss [43]. Gradient boosting generalises this view to any differentiable loss: each new tree is fitted to the negative gradient of the loss with respect to the current predictions (for squared error, simply the residuals), and is added with a small learning rate [37]:

Regularised, highly optimised implementations such as XGBoost are among the most accurate off-the-shelf methods for tabular data [41,42].

8Support vector machines

When two classes are linearly separable, infinitely many hyperplanes separate them. The support vector machine picks the one with the largest margin, the distance to the nearest training points [31,32]. With labels and the scaling chosen so that the closest points satisfy , the margin equals . Maximising it while allowing slack for points inside the margin or misclassified gives the soft-margin problem [32]:

Eliminating shows that this is the same as minimising the hinge loss plus an L2 penalty, which places the SVM within the regularised ERM framework of Section 1 [2]. The constant sets the trade-off: large penalises violations heavily and gives a narrow margin; small gives a wider margin and a smoother classifier.

The kernel trick

In the dual form of the problem the data enter only through inner products :

Replacing the inner product with a kernel fits a linear separator in a high- or even infinite-dimensional feature space without ever computing [31,47]. Common choices are the polynomial kernel and the Gaussian radial basis function (RBF) kernel . Only points with contribute to ; these are the support vectors [3,32]. Support vector regression applies the same ideas with an -insensitive loss [6].

9Neural networks

A feed-forward neural network, or multilayer perceptron (MLP), composes several layers, each an affine map followed by a non-linear activation [45]:

The output function is the identity for regression (with squared loss) and the softmax for classification (with cross-entropy). Without the non-linearity the whole network would collapse to a single linear map. The rectified linear unit is the most common modern choice [45,48]. With enough hidden units, a network with a single hidden layer can approximate any continuous function on a compact set to arbitrary accuracy [29,30]. This guarantees that a suitable network exists but says nothing about how to find it or how much data that takes.

Training minimises the empirical risk by mini-batch stochastic gradient descent or an adaptive variant such as Adam [46], with gradients supplied by back-propagation [28]. The objective is non-convex, but in practice large networks trained this way generalise well, especially when combined with regularisers such as weight decay, early stopping and dropout, which randomly zeroes units during training [45,49]. Architectures that build in structure, such as convolutional networks for images, are what made deep learning dominant on perceptual tasks [39,40].

10Generalisation: bias, variance and regularisation

The bias–variance decomposition

Suppose with and , and let be fitted to a random training set. At a fixed point , the expected squared prediction error, averaged over training sets and noise, splits into three parts [2,50]:

Simple models (a straight line fitted to a curve) have high bias: on average they miss the truth. Flexible models (a degree-12 polynomial through 20 points) have low bias but high variance: they change a lot from one training set to another. Test error is minimised at an intermediate complexity, while training error keeps falling as complexity grows (Figure 9). Training error is therefore an optimistic estimate of test error [2,4].

The classical U-shaped curve is not the whole story. Very over-parameterised models, such as large neural networks and random forests, can interpolate the training data and still generalise well. Past the point where the model can fit the data exactly, test error can fall a second time, a phenomenon called double descent [51].

Regularisation: ridge, lasso and elastic net

Regularisation adds a penalty on the size of the parameters to the training loss, deliberately adding a little bias in exchange for a large cut in variance. For linear regression the two classic penalties are:

Ridge regression shrinks all coefficients toward zero and makes the problem well conditioned even when features are highly correlated or [23]. The lasso's L1 penalty sets some coefficients exactly to zero, so it performs variable selection at the same time as estimation [33]. The geometry explains why: the L1 constraint region has corners on the axes, and the elliptical contours of the squared loss usually first touch it at a corner (Figure 10). The elastic net mixes the two penalties and behaves better than the lasso when groups of features are correlated [52]. The penalty strength is a hyperparameter chosen by cross-validation, and features should be standardised first so that the penalty treats them equally [2]. In Bayesian terms, ridge and lasso estimates are the posterior modes under Gaussian and Laplace priors on respectively [3,33].

11Evaluating models

Hold-out sets and cross-validation

Because training error is optimistic, performance must be measured on data the model did not see during fitting. With plenty of data, a common design splits it into training, validation and test sets (Figure 1). With less data, k-fold cross-validation (CV) is more efficient: the data are divided into folds, each fold in turn serves as the validation set for a model trained on the other , and the error estimates are averaged (Figure 11) [2,24]. In an extensive empirical study, Kohavi recommended stratified 10-fold CV, which keeps class proportions the same in every fold, for model selection [53].

Two mistakes are common and serious. Data leakage occurs when information from the validation or test data reaches the training process, for example by standardising features or selecting features on the full dataset before splitting. It produces estimates that are too optimistic and models that fail in deployment [2,54]. The fix is to put every data-dependent step inside a pipeline that is re-fitted within each training fold. Second, if the same CV loop both tunes hyperparameters and reports performance, the reported error is biased downward. Nested cross-validation, with an inner loop for tuning and an outer loop for assessment, removes this bias [55].

Metrics for classification

For a binary classifier, the confusion matrix counts true positives (TP), false positives (FP), true negatives (TN) and false negatives (FN). The main metrics follow from it [56]:

Accuracy can mislead when classes are imbalanced: if 1% of transactions are fraudulent, a model that never predicts fraud is 99% accurate and useless. Most classifiers output a score, and a threshold turns it into a label. The ROC curve plots TPR against FPR as the threshold varies, and the area under it (AUC) equals the probability that a randomly chosen positive is scored above a randomly chosen negative [56]. When positives are rare, precision–recall curves are often more informative; one curve dominates another in ROC space if and only if it dominates in precision–recall space [57].

12End-to-end examples

Classification: comparing seven models

The Wisconsin diagnostic breast cancer dataset contains 569 tumours described by 30 features computed from digitised images of fine-needle aspirates, each labelled malignant or benign [58]. It ships with scikit-learn, where the label 1 means benign [38]. Listing 4 compares the model families from this article with stratified 10-fold CV. Models that depend on distances or on the scale of the weights are wrapped in a pipeline with StandardScaler, so that scaling is re-fitted inside each training fold and nothing leaks.

On this dataset logistic regression is as good as anything else and ties with the RBF-kernel SVM: once the features are standardised, the classes are close to linearly separable. A single unpruned tree is clearly worst, and the two tree ensembles recover most of the gap, as the variance argument in Section 7 predicts. The standard deviations across folds (about ±0.02) are as large as most of the differences between the top models, so the ranking among them should not be over-interpreted.

Regression: regularisation on the diabetes data

The diabetes dataset records ten baseline variables (age, sex, body mass index, blood pressure and six blood serum measurements) for 442 patients, with a quantitative measure of disease progression one year later as the target [59]. Listing 5 tunes ridge and lasso penalties by 5-fold CV inside the training set, then scores every model once on a held-out test set.

All the linear models explain about 36% of the variance on the test set. The lasso does about as well as OLS while using only seven of the ten features, a simpler model at almost no cost in accuracy. Here the random forest is worse than the linear models, a reminder that more flexible models need more data, and that the right model depends on the problem [8].

Exercise 9. Spot the leak Practice

An analyst has 200 samples and 10,000 gene-expression features. They (1) pick the 50 features most correlated with the label using all 200 samples, then (2) run 10-fold CV of a classifier on those 50 features and report 95% accuracy. What is wrong, and how should it be done?

Solution

Feature selection used the labels of every sample, including those that later serve as validation folds, so information about the validation labels leaked into training. With 10,000 features, some will correlate with the label by chance even if the labels are pure noise, and the CV estimate can look excellent when the true accuracy is at chance level. Hastie, Tibshirani and Friedman call this the "wrong way" to do cross-validation [2].

The correct procedure repeats feature selection inside each training fold, using only that fold's training data, and then evaluates on the held-out fold. If the number of features or other hyperparameters are tuned as well, use nested CV [55]. In scikit-learn, put the selector and the classifier in one Pipeline and cross-validate the pipeline [38,54].

Exercise 10. Cross-validation from scratch Code

Write a function that estimates the accuracy of a k-NN classifier by 5-fold cross-validation using only NumPy, standardising the features correctly inside each fold. Use it to choose from on the breast cancer data.

Solution

The key line fits the mean and standard deviation on the training fold only and applies them to both folds.

Accuracy rises from (high variance) to a peak at , then falls slowly as the boundary becomes too smooth (more bias), which is the bias–variance trade-off of Section 10 in miniature. The differences are within about one standard deviation, so any between 3 and 15 is a reasonable choice. Exact figures depend on the random fold assignment.
